references.text: Isaiah's parable of the vineyard in [ref:Jes 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1-7] is the Old Testament background for Jesus' parable. Isaiah describes how the Lord planted a vineyard (Israel) and expected fruit, but it yielded wild grapes. Jesus builds on this image but shifts attention to the tenants (the leaders) who do not give the owner the harvest.

The parallel text in [ref:Matt 21:33-41|Matthew 21:33-41] gives Matthew's version of the same parable about the vineyard and the wicked tenants, with several details drawn from Isaiah 5, such as the fence, the winepress, and the watchtower.

The parallel text in [ref:Mark 12:1-9|Mark 12:1-9] is Mark's version of the same parable. Mark also includes details about the fence, the winepress, and the tower, following a similar narrative about the servants who were mistreated.

In [ref:Sal 80:9-17|Psalm 80:9-17], Israel is described as a vine that God brought out of Egypt and planted in the promised land. This psalm uses the same image of God planting a vineyard, which underlies the parable in Luke 20:9.

In [ref:Jer 2:21|Jeremiah 2:21], the Lord says: "I planted you as a choice vine," but Israel turned away. This is part of the prophetic tradition of Israel as God's vineyard, which Jesus takes up in his parable.

In [ref:Luk 19:11-12|Luke 19:11-12], Jesus tells the parable about a man of noble birth who went to a distant country. The motif of an owner traveling away for a long time (ἀπεδήμησεν χρόνους ἱκανούς) thematically connects the two parables.
In [ref:Høys 8:11-12|Song of Solomon 8:11-12], a vineyard is mentioned that Solomon leased to keepers, a motif that parallels the owner in Jesus' parable who leased his vineyard to tenants.
